entries.why_wrong: The outer check isn't the problem — it's actually the whole point of the pattern, letting most calls skip the synchronized block once `instance` is set. Removing it would force every call through synchronization forever, which is a performance regression, not a fix; the real defect is that the field lacks `volatile` so the outer read can see a half-built object.

There's no `this` to synchronize on here — `getInstance()` is a static method, so `this` doesn't exist and synchronizing on the class object (`Singleton.class`) is the correct way to lock across all threads calling it. The actual issue isn't which monitor is used; it's that `instance` isn't `volatile`, letting a thread read a reference before the constructor's writes are visible.

This doesn't deadlock: `synchronized` blocks threads competing for the same lock one at a time, and each thread releases the lock as soon as it exits the block, so there's no circular wait or held-and-wait condition. The real hazard is visibility, not locking — without `volatile`, a thread can see a non-null `instance` whose constructor hasn't finished running.

Returning a fresh instance every call would defeat the entire purpose of a singleton — caching one shared instance is the intended behavior, not a flaw. The bug isn't about whether the instance is reused; it's that `instance` isn't `volatile`, so a thread can observe the cached reference before the object it points to is fully initialized.
